claim: The Mexican tetra, Astyanax mexicanus, exists in two morphs: eyed surface-dwelling populations and blind cave populations.
source: A. mexicanus exists in two morphs: (1) eyed surface-dwelling populations and (2) blind cave populations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a fundamental characteristic of the species.

claim: There are at least 30 independently evolved cavefish populations in the caves of the Sierra de El Abra region of Northeast Mexico.
source: There are at least 30 independently evolved cavefish populations in the caves of the Sierra de El Abra region of Northeast Mexico (Espinasa et al., 2018; Herman et al., 2018; McGaugh et al., 2020; Mitchell et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: A. mexicanus populations are interfertile.
source: A. mexicanus populations are interfertile, and this attribute has allowed investigators to demonstrate independent convergence of numerous behavioral, developmental, and physiological traits (Chin et al., 2018; Kowalko, 2020; Riddle et al., 2018; Stockdale et al., 2018; Varatharasan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations showing how this property has been used in research.

claim: The mechanoreceptive hair cells of the lateral line system detect fluid motion relative to the body and play an important role in essential behaviors.
source: The mechanoreceptive hair cells of the lateral line system detects fluid motion relative to the body and play an important role in essential behaviors (McHenry et al., 2009; Mekdara et al., 2018; Olszewski et al., 2012; Oteiza et al., 2017; Stewart et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on lateral line function.

claim: Cavefish have evolved anatomical enhancements of the lateral line, presumably to compensate for the loss of vision.
source: Cavefish have evolved anatomical enhancements of the lateral line, presumably to compensate for the loss of vision (Kowalko, 2020; McGaugh et al., 2020; Teyke, 1990; Yoshizawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and includes a speculative element about the compensatory function.

claim: Anatomical alterations of the lateral line in cavefish have been linked to substantial changes in behavior.
source: These anatomical alterations have been linked to substantial changes in behavior (Lloyd et al., 2018; Yoshizawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Spontaneous spikes from auditory hair cells enable precise encoding of much higher frequencies.
source: For example, the spontaneous spikes from auditory hair cells have been shown to enable precise encoding of much higher frequencies (Köppl, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Spontaneous depolarizing currents within the hair cell maintain a resting potential within the critical activation range of channels, which is required to ensure transmitter release and decrease the detection threshold of the system.
source: In the lateral line, spontaneous depolarizing currents within the hair cell maintain a resting potential within the critical activation range of channels. This range is required to ensure transmitter release; thus these currents decrease the detection threshold of the system (Trapani and Nicolson, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Hindbrain efferent neurons issue predictive signals that transmit in parallel to locomotor commands, termed corollary discharge.
source: More specifically, hindbrain efferent neurons (hereafter 'efferents') issue predictive signals that transmit in parallel to locomotor commands, termed corollary discharge (CD).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about neural mechanisms.

claim: Corollary discharges inhibit afferent activity to mitigate sensor fatigue that can result from self-generated stimuli.
source: CDs inhibit afferent activity to mitigate sensor fatigue that can result from self-generated stimuli (Russell and Roberts, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Active-flow sensing by cavefish depends on detecting reafferent signals while swimming.
source: For example, active-flow sensing by cavefish depends on detecting reafferent signals while swimming (Tan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Pachón cavefish exhibit a significant increase in anterior neuromast quantity as early as 6 dpf compared to surface fish.
source: Here, we show that Pachón cavefish exhibit this significant increase in anterior neuromast quantity as early as 6 dpf (p < 0.01, t = 3.168, df = 29; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Both surface and Pachón populations exhibit a similar number of posterior lateral line neuromasts.
source: In contrast, both populations exhibit a similar number of posterior lateral line neuromasts (p = 0.77, U = 111.5; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Neuromasts along the posterior lateral line were comprised of similar quantities of hair cells across blind and surface morphs.
source: Neuromasts along the posterior lateral line were comprised of similar quantities of hair cells across blind (n = 11) and surface morphs (n = 9; p = 0.09; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 1F.

claim: No significant interaction was detected between the effects of population and age (5–7 dpf) on hair cell counts.
source: No significant interaction was detected between the effects of population and age (5–7 dpf; F2,72 = 2.96, p = 0.06; Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 1G.

claim: Intrinsic spontaneous activity was higher in Pachón cavefish (18.6 ± 0.2 Hz) while the animal was at rest, relative to surface fish (12.4 ± 0.3 Hz).
source: Extracellular recordings of posterior lateral line afferents revealed intrinsic spontaneous activity was higher in Pachón cavefish (18.6 ± 0.2 Hz) while the animal was at rest, relative to surface fish (12.4 ± 0.3 Hz; p < 0.01, t = 15.97, df = 5,795; Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Evoked afferent activity at 30 Hz was statistically elevated in Pachón cavefish (119.6 ± 16.6 Hz) relative to surface fish (73.2 ± 6.9 Hz).
source: The neuromasts were stimulated at different frequencies (5–40 Hz) and a pairwise comparison of evoked afferent activity at 30 Hz revealed statistically elevated spike rates in Pachón cavefish (n = 12; 119.6 ± 16.6 Hz) relative to surface fish (n = 10; 73.2 ± 6.9 Hz; p = 0.03, t = 2.38, df = 18; Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental stimulation data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: Significantly elevated spike rates were detected in response to a 40-Hz stimulus in Pachón cavefish (101.3 ± 13.6 Hz) relative to surface fish (52.3 ± 7.0 Hz).
source: Significantly elevated spike rates were also detected in response to a 40-Hz stimulus in Pachón cavefish (101.3 ± 13.6 Hz) relative to surface fish (52.3 ± 7.0 Hz; p < 0.01, t = 3.00, df = 18; Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental stimulation data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: Spontaneous afferent activity is a reliable metric for estimating the sensitivity of the lateral line.
source: Together these findings support spontaneous afferent activity as a reliable metric for estimating the sensitivity of the lateral line and reveal enhanced neural responses to hair cell deflection in cavefish.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results presented.

claim: Swim bouts of longer duration were observed in surface fish (357 ± 5 ms) when compared to Pachón cavefish (264 ± 4 ms).
source: Swim bouts of longer duration were observed in surface fish (357 ± 5 ms; n = 3167 swim bouts) when compared to Pachón cavefish (264 ± 4 ms; n = 2612 swim bouts; p < 0.01, t-stat = 15.2, df = 5777).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: During most surface fish swim bouts there was a reduction in afferent activity (85.8%), with many resulting in complete quiescence of transmissions (48.5%).
source: During most surface fish swim bouts there was a reduction in afferent activity (n = 1966/2291, 85.8%), many of which resulted in complete quiescence of transmissions (n = 1112/2291, 48.5%).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Afferent activity partially reduced during many swim bouts in Pachón cavefish (53.4%), but very few instances led to complete inhibition (11.3%).
source: Conversely, afferent activity partially reduced during many swim bouts in Pachón cavefish (n = 1303/2439, 53.4%), but very few instances led to complete inhibition (n = 275/2439, 11.3%).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Surface fish experience significantly higher levels of inhibition (68.5 ± 0.01%) compared to cavefish (28.9 ± 0.01%) during swimming.
source: Therefore, surface fish experience significantly higher levels of inhibition (68.5 ± 0.01%) compared to cavefish (28.9 ± 0.01%; p < 0.01, t = 36.5, df = 4449; Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Surface fish demonstrate lateral line inhibition during swimming comparable to other fishes with intact visual systems.
source: Surface fish demonstrate lateral line inhibition during swimming comparable to other fishes with intact visual systems (Flock and Russell, 1973; Lunsford et al., 2019; Pichler and Lagnado, 2020; Russell and Roberts, 1972) suggesting cavefish have evolved a unique functional phenotype for sensory gain control.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research and includes an inference about cavefish evolution.

claim: Backfilled efferents revealed similar soma quantities between surface fish (2.4±0.3) and cavefish (3.2±0.5).
source: Between populations, backfilled efferents revealed similar soma quantities (surface: 2.4±0.3; cave: 3.2±0.5; p = 0.2, t = 1.36, df = 18) and size (surface: 62.1 ± 3.6 µm2; cave: 70.9 ± 4.5 µm2; p = 0.1, t = 1.50, df = 51; Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical measurements and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 4A-C.

claim: Efferent soma size was similar between surface fish (62.1 ± 3.6 µm2) and cavefish (70.9 ± 4.5 µm2).
source: Between populations, backfilled efferents revealed similar soma quantities (surface: 2.4±0.3; cave: 3.2±0.5; p = 0.2, t = 1.36, df = 18) and size (surface: 62.1 ± 3.6 µm2; cave: 70.9 ± 4.5 µm2; p = 0.1, t = 1.50, df = 51; Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical measurements and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 4A-C.

claim: In control surface fish, average spike rates during and prior to a swim were not positively correlated, but the slope indicates a fractional suppression of 78%.
source: From electrophysiological recordings, we observed average spike rates during and prior to a swim were not positively correlated in control surface fish (r2=0.15, F1,13 = 2.3, p = 0.2), but the slope of the line indicates a fractional suppression of 78% that is significantly less than unity (slope 0.1, confidence interval [CI]: −0.2 to 0.4; Figure 4Di).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data and reference to Figure 4Di.

claim: In efferent-ablated surface fish, spike rates during swimming intervals were indistinguishable from those during nonswimming intervals, showing no detectable inhibitory effect.
source: In the efferent-ablated surface fish, the spike rates during swimming intervals were indistinguishable from those during nonswimming intervals (slope 1.2, CI = −0.1 to 2.4) showing no detectable inhibitory effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data from ablation experiments.

claim: Putative cholinergic hindbrain efferents are necessary for afferent inhibition in surface fish, but do not demonstrate modulatory control of afferents in cavefish.
source: Therefore, putative cholinergic hindbrain efferents are necessary for afferent inhibition in surface fish, but do not demonstrate modulatory control of afferents in cavefish.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ablation experiments comparing surface fish and cavefish.

claim: Surface fish afferent spike rates during swimming (3.9 ± 0.1 Hz) were 71% lower than the immediate pre-swim period in control fish (13.7 ± 0.2 Hz).
source: Surface fish afferent spike rates during swimming (3.9 ± 0.1 Hz) were 71% lower than the immediate pre-swim period in control fish (13.7 ± 0.2 Hz; Tukey's post hoc test, p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: In control Pachón cavefish, afferent spike rate during swimming (16.8 ± 0.2 Hz) was not statistically discriminated from pre-swim (20.5 ± 0.2 Hz).
source: In control Pachón cavefish, we observed some decrease in afferent spike rate during swimming (16.8 ± 0.2 Hz) but it was not statistically discriminated from pre-swim (20.5 ± 0.2 Hz; Tukey's post hoc test, p = 0.94).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Efferent ablation in surface fish resulted in afferent activity during swimming (17.4 ± 0.3 Hz) to increase to pre-swim levels (20.7 ± 0.3 Hz).
source: Efferent ablation in surface fish resulted in afferent activity during swimming (17.4 ± 0.3 Hz) to increase to pre-swim levels (20.7 ± 0.3 Hz; Tukey's post hoc test, p = 0.99).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data from ablation experiments.

claim: Efferents are necessary for inhibition of afferents during swimming in surface fish.
source: These findings indicate that efferents are necessary for inhibition of afferents during swimming in surface fish.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ablation experiments.

claim: Blind cavefish populations exhibited similar spontaneous spike rates across populations (Pachón, Tinaja, and Molino).
source: Blind cavefish populations exhibited similar spontaneous spike rates across populations (F2,17 = 0.68, p = 0.52), and swimming showed little effect on lateral line activity across blind cavefish populations (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The relative change in afferent spike rates (inhibition) was similar in Pachón (0.28 ± 0.01) and Tinaja (0.32 ± 0.02).
source: We observed a minor decrease in afferent spike rates across cavefish populations and the relative change (i.e., inhibition) was similar in Pachón and Tinaja (Tukey's post hoc test; Pachón: 0.28 ± 0.01; Tinaja: 0.32 ± 0.02; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data and reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Molino demonstrated an intermediate phenotype compared to Pachón and Tinaja (inhibition: 0.23 ± 0.01).
source: Molino demonstrated an intermediate phenotype compared to Pachón and Tinaja (Tukey's post hoc test; Molino: 0.23 ± 0.01; p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The Molino population (new lineage) is most distantly related to the Pachón and Tinaja populations (old lineage), originating from a more recent surface fish colonization of caves.
source: The Molino population (new lineage) is most distantly related to the Pachón and Tinaja populations (old lineage), originating from a more recent surface fish colonization of caves thus providing phylogenetic evidence that coincides with statistically similar groupings (Herman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published phylogenetic research.

claim: Afferent spike rates during swimming were not statistically distinguishable from unity across all cave populations (Pachón, Tinaja, and Molino).
source: Spike rates during swimming and pre-swim intervals were positively correlated in all cave populations, and afferent spike rates during swimming were not statistically distinguishable from unity across populations (Pachón: slope = 0.88, CI = −0.5 to 2.2; Tinaja: slope = 1.03, CI = −0.2 to 2.2; Molino: slope = 1.02, CI = 0.8 to 1.2; Figure 5D), indicating there was no significant decrease in afferent activity during swimming within blind cavefish populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data and reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Elevated lateral line afferent activity and loss of efferent function have repeatedly evolved together across cavefish populations.
source: By employing neurophysiological approaches in the lateral line system of A. mexicanus for the first time, we show that elevated lateral line afferent activity and loss of efferent function have repeatedly evolved together across cavefish populations.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the experimental results across multiple populations.

claim: The increased afferent activity in cavefish is a likely consequence of eye loss.
source: The increased afferent activity in cavefish is a likely consequence of eye loss, which has robust effects on other physiological systems (Duboué et al., 2011; Varatharasan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to research on physiological effects of eye loss.

claim: Heightened lateral line sensitivity in adults has been previously attributed to increased neuromast density in the anterior lateral line as well as increased hair cell quantities per neuromast.
source: Heightened lateral line sensitivity in adults has been previously attributed to increased neuromast density in the ALL as well as increased hair cell quantities per neuromast (Jaggard et al., 2017; Lloyd et al., 2018; McHenry et al., 2008; Patton et al., 2010; Teyke, 1990; Yoffe et al., 2020; Yoffe et al., 2020; Yoshizawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The increased spontaneous activity that contributes to the enhanced evoked responses in cavefish is a powerful addition for flow sensing.
source: Our discovery of increased spontaneous activity that contributes to the enhanced evoked responses in cavefish is a powerful addition for flow sensing, and we predict that this in combination with the increased number of neuromasts in the ALL (Yoshizawa et al., 2010) is what ultimately enables cavefish to perform active-flow sensing.
evidence: This is an inference and prediction based on the experimental findings.

claim: Three blind populations of cavefish (Pachón, Molino, and Tinaja) have repeatedly lost the capability for efferent modulation during swimming.
source: We found that three blind populations of cavefish (i.e., Pachón, Molino, and Tinaja) have repeatedly lost the capability for efferent modulation during swimming.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results across multiple populations.

claim: Lateral line efferent activity can be driven by direct inputs from the visual system in zebrafish.
source: When one considers that lateral line efferent activity can be driven by direct inputs from the visual system in zebrafish (Reinig et al., 2017), it seems possible that eye degeneration induces the loss of efferent function.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and is used to support a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Lateral line efferents are thought to have undergone regressive loss in the ancestral lamprey and hagfish.
source: This interpretation is consistent with the idea that lateral line efferents are thought to have undergone regressive loss before in the ancestral lamprey and hagfish (Kishida et al., 1987; Köppl, 2011; Koyama et al., 1990), both of which are nearly or completely blind during development (Dickson and Collard, 1979; Fernholm and Holmberg, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The cholinergic efferent system is still present in cavefish, having lost functionality rather than disappearing.
source: However, our results illustrate that cholinergic efferent system is still present in cavefish, having lost functionality rather than disappearing (the efferent system is functional in surface fish).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical and functional data presented.

claim: Active-flow sensing occurs during swimming and involves using the reflection of self-generated flow fields to follow walls, avoid obstacles, and discriminate between shapes.
source: Active-flow sensing occurs during swimming and involves using the reflection of self-generated flow fields (Bleckmann et al., 1991) to follow walls (Patton et al., 2010), avoid obstacles (Teyke, 1985; Windsor et al., 2008), and discrimination between shapes (de Perera, 2004; Hassan, 1989; von Campenhausen et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The repeated loss of inhibition across populations at the larval stage suggests that selection may act early in development on the efferent over afferent systems.
source: The repeated loss of inhibition across populations at the larval stage suggests that selection may act early in development on the efferent over afferent systems.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cavefish swim by using different body motions than surface fish, which has been interpreted as a mechanism to enhance wall following.
source: Cavefish swim by using different body motions than surface fish. This finding has been interpreted as a mechanism to enhance wall following, which occurs when the bow wake of a swimming cavefish is reflected off of a solid surface and then detected (Patton et al., 2010; Sharma et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Altered swimming kinematics in cavefish are thought to have arisen from a general increase in sensitivity to flow.
source: Altered swimming kinematics are also thought to have arisen from a general increase in sensitivity to flow (Tan et al., 2011; Windsor et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The lack of efferent function in cavefish precludes the sensory feedback necessary for sensing self-movement and body position in water (proprioception).
source: Our results provide an alternate suggestion; the lack of efferent function in cavefish precludes the sensory feedback necessary for sensing self-movement and body position in water (proprioception).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Corollary discharge plays a critical role in swimming efficiency by enabling the tracking of the traveling body wave during undulation.
source: CD, a parallel motor command that decreases the afferent activity of fishes when swimming, has recently been found to play a critical role in swimming efficiency by enabling the tracking of the traveling body wave during undulation (Skandalis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The evolved loss of efferent function that enables cavefish to successfully avoid collisions in subterranean habitats is likely favored over optimizing swimming efficiency.
source: We hypothesize that the evolved loss of efferent function that enables cavefish to successfully avoid collisions in subterranean habitats is likely favored over optimizing swimming efficiency (Nakamura, 1997; Atasavun Uysal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Loss of efferent function will be found in other blind hypogean species.
source: We predict that loss of efferent function will be found in other blind hypogean species (Costa Sampaio et al., 2012) and that their respective surface populations will possess intact efferent functionality, as we have found in A. mexicanus.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the findings in A. mexicanus.

claim: Anterior lateral line neuromasts had previously been shown to differ in quantities and morphology as early as 2 months post fertilization between surface and cavefish.
source: Anterior lateral line (ALL) neuromasts had previously been shown to differ in quantities and morphology as early as 2 months post fertilization between surface and cavefish (Yoshizawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The posterior lateral line was exclusively probed to establish whether sensory systems that are anatomically similar exhibit neurophysiological differences that contribute to enhanced sensitivity.
source: We exclusively probed the posterior lateral line afferent neurons to establish whether sensory systems that are anatomically similar exhibit neurophysiological differences that contribute to enhanced sensitivity.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and rationale.

claim: Extracellular recordings of posterior lateral line afferents were adapted from protocols used in zebrafish.
source: To examine the physiological basis of differences in lateral line function across surface and cavefish we used extracellular lateral line recordings adapted from protocols used in zebrafish (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The Tinaja and Pachón populations are derived from similarly timed colonization events.
source: We compared lateral line activity between three different cave populations (Figure 5A); the Tinaja and Pachón populations, which are derived from similarly timed colonization events, and the Molino population that is derived from a more recent colonization event (Bradic et al., 2012; Dowling et al., 2002; Herman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published phylogenetic research.

claim: The Molino population is derived from a more recent colonization event than Pachón and Tinaja.
source: We compared lateral line activity between three different cave populations (Figure 5A); the Tinaja and Pachón populations, which are derived from similarly timed colonization events, and the Molino population that is derived from a more recent colonization event (Bradic et al., 2012; Dowling et al., 2002; Herman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published phylogenetic research.

claim: Three independently derived cavefish populations have evolved persistent afferent activity during locomotion.
source: We discovered that three independently derived cavefish populations have evolved persistent afferent activity during locomotion, suggesting for the first time that partial loss of function in the efferent system can be an evolutionary mechanism for neural adaptation of a vertebrate sensory system.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study based on experimental data across multiple populations.

claim: Partial loss of function in the efferent system can be an evolutionary mechanism for neural adaptation of a vertebrate sensory system.
source: We discovered that three independently derived cavefish populations have evolved persistent afferent activity during locomotion, suggesting for the first time that partial loss of function in the efferent system can be an evolutionary mechanism for neural adaptation of a vertebrate sensory system.
evidence: This is a novel inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Elevated endogenous afferent activity identified a lower response threshold in the lateral line of blind cavefish relative to surface fish.
source: Elevated endogenous afferent activity identified a lower response threshold in the lateral line of blind cavefish relative to surface fish leading to increased evoked potentials during hair cell deflection in cavefish.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental measurements of spontaneous and evoked activity.

claim: Elevated endogenous afferent activity leads to increased evoked potentials during hair cell deflection in cavefish.
source: Elevated endogenous afferent activity identified a lower response threshold in the lateral line of blind cavefish relative to surface fish leading to increased evoked potentials during hair cell deflection in cavefish.
evidence: This is an inference connecting spontaneous activity to evoked responses based on experimental data.

claim: Differences in intrinsic afferent signaling and gain control exist across A. mexicanus populations.
source: These studies indicate differences in intrinsic afferent signaling and gain control across populations.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings from the neurophysiological studies.

claim: Higher spontaneous activity is one of two mechanisms responsible for higher lateral line sensitivity in cavefish.
source: Higher spontaneous activity is one of two mechanisms that are responsible for higher lateral line sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The inhibitory effects of the efferent system during swimming is a feedback mechanism conserved across the diversity of fishes.
source: The other involves the inhibitory effects of the efferent system during swimming, a feedback mechanism that is conserved across the diversity of fishes (Flock and Russell, 1973; Lunsford et al., 2019; Montgomery et al., 1996; Montgomery and Bodznick, 1994; Roberts and Russell, 1972; Tricas and Highstein, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The inhibitory feedback mechanism is true in swimming surface fish but not in cavefish.
source: This is true in swimming surface fish but not in cavefish.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results comparing surface fish and cavefish.
